posts.title: Turn an agent failure into a regression evaluation
posts.body: Capture a specific failure and make it a test you can rerun after changing the workflow. For example, if a support agent claims a refund succeeded after a tool error, preserve that scenario and check that the next version reports the failure accurately.

posts.title: Why PagedAttention fixed KV cache fragmentation
posts.body:
Preallocating the maximum context per request wastes most of GPU memory. Paging the KV cache into fixed blocks removes that waste.
- Blocks are allocated on demand and need not be contiguous.
- Requests that share a prefix can share blocks copy-on-write.
👉 Throughput gains come from packing more concurrent requests, not from faster math.

posts.title: Speculative decoding keeps the output distribution exact
posts.body:
A small draft model proposes several tokens. The large model verifies them in one forward pass.
- Accepted tokens use rejection sampling, so the distribution matches the large model.
- Speedup depends on the acceptance rate, not on the draft model's raw quality alone.
👉 A draft that is cheap and well aligned beats a bigger draft.

posts.title: ReAct is an observation loop, not a chain
posts.body:
An agent interleaves a model step with a tool call, then feeds the tool result back into the next step.
- The loop only works if observations are short, structured, and truthful.
- Without a step budget, it can repeat the same failing call forever.
👉 Track repeated (tool, args) pairs and stop after the second identical failure.

posts.title: Building an agent loop you can trust
posts.body:
Five guardrails that separate a demo agent from one you can run unattended.
👉 Swipe for the checklist.

slides.title: Bound the loop
slides.body: Set a max step count and a max token and cost budget per task. Stop with a clear status when either is hit.

slides.title: Validate every call
slides.body:
- Check arguments against a schema
- Reject tools the task does not need
- Scope credentials per tool

slides.title: Make side effects safe
slides.body: Use idempotency keys on writes. Require explicit confirmation for irreversible actions.
slides.code:
key = hash(task_id, tool, args)
if seen(key): return cached_result

slides.title: Trace everything
slides.body: Store each step as a span: prompt, tool call, observation, and decision. You need this to debug the run you did not expect.

slides.title: Takeaway
slides.body: **An agent is a loop with a budget.** Reliability comes from limits and logs, not from a better prompt.

posts.title: Tools are APIs the model calls, so treat them like one
posts.body:
The model will send malformed or repeated arguments. Your tool layer has to defend against that.
- Validate arguments against a schema before executing anything.
- Make side-effecting tools idempotent, so a retried call does not double-charge or double-send.
👉 A retry policy without idempotency keys turns one agent mistake into two real actions.

posts.title: Plan first when the workflow is known
posts.body:
Re-planning every step is costly and makes behavior hard to predict. A fixed plan is cheap when the steps are known.
- Use a planner for a known workflow, then execute steps with narrow tools.
- Let the agent re-plan only on an explicit failure signal.
👉 Hybrid is the common production shape: plan upfront, react at the failure points.

posts.title: Evaluate agent trajectories, not final answers
posts.body:
Two agents can give the same answer with very different paths. The path shows the cost, the risk, and the failure modes.
- Log every tool call, argument, and observation with a trace id.
- Score task success, steps taken, and unsafe actions separately.
👉 If you only grade the final string, you will ship agents that succeed by luck.

posts.title: Most multi-agent systems should be one agent with tools
posts.body:
Splitting work across agents adds coordination, context loss at each handoff, and more places to fail.
- Split only when roles need different tools, permissions, or context windows.
- Otherwise one agent with well-named tools is easier to debug.
👉 Count the handoffs before you add the second agent.

posts.title: Patch size sets the compute budget of a ViT
posts.body:
Self-attention cost grows with the square of the token count. Halving the patch side quadruples the tokens and roughly multiplies attention cost by 16.
- Smaller patches keep fine detail but explode the sequence length.
- Higher resolution at a fixed patch size costs the same way.
👉 Choose patch size from the smallest object you must detect, then budget resolution.
